subject: anatomy
title: Otic Ganglion, Pterygoid Venous Plexus, and Muscles of Mastication

steps.tx: The otic ganglion is a peripheral parasympathetic ganglion situated in the infratemporal fossa immediately below the foramen ovale. Topographically, the **otic ganglion** is intimately related to the trunk of the mandibular nerve, lying on its medial surface sandwiched against the tensor veli palatini muscle. Functionally, it relays secretomotor impulses to the parotid gland.
steps.say: Located below foramen ovale, the otic ganglion rests on the medial aspect of the mandibular nerve trunk. Functionally, it serves as the parasympathetic relay for the parotid gland.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic showing the position and roots of the otic ganglion in the infratemporal space
vis.caption: Topographical location of the otic ganglion and parasympathetic secretomotor relay pathways. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The otic ganglion receives three distinct functional roots. Its parasympathetic motor root is formed by the lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX), which synapses within the ganglion. Its sympathetic root derives from the plexus on the middle meningeal artery (vasoconstrictor). Crucially, motor fibres from the **nerve to medial pterygoid** pass directly through the ganglion without synapsing to innervate tensor veli palatini and tensor tympani.
steps.say: The otic ganglion receives parasympathetic, sympathetic, and sensory roots. Motor fibres from the mandibular nerve pass through without synapsing to innervate tensor veli palatini and tensor tympani.

Sympathetic

steps.tx: Surrounding and infiltrating the lateral pterygoid muscle in the infratemporal fossa is the pterygoid venous plexus, an extensive, valveless venous rete. The **pterygoid plexus** collects venous tributaries that correspond to the branches of the maxillary artery, ultimately coalescing posteriorly to form the short maxillary vein, which drains into the retromandibular vein.
steps.say: The pterygoid venous plexus surrounds the lateral pterygoid muscle. Collecting blood from masticatory tissues, it drains posteriorly into the maxillary vein.

nodes.label: Masticatory and Dental Inflow (Receives deep temporal, alveolar, and meningeal veins)
Pterygoid Venous Plexus (Intricate venous meshwork embedding lateral pterygoid)
Maxillary Vein (Unites with superficial temporal to form retromandibular vein)
Retromandibular Vein (Main venous exit from infratemporal fossa)

steps.tx: Because the pterygoid venous plexus is entirely valveless, it serves as an anatomical crossroads linking superficial facial veins with deep intracranial sinuses. It communicates with the facial vein via the deep facial vein, and with the **cavernous sinus** through emissary veins traversing foramen ovale and foramen lacerum. Septic odontogenic infections can track through this network into cavernous sinus thrombosis.
steps.say: Lacking valves, the pterygoid plexus communicates with the facial vein and cavernous sinus. Infected emboli from lower molar abscesses can track retrogradely into the skull.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic showing venous connections between pterygoid venous plexus and intracranial cavernous sinus
vis.caption: Emissary venous communications connecting the infratemporal pterygoid plexus to the intracranial cavernous sinus. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The four classic muscles of mastication develop from the mesoderm of the first pharyngeal arch and are innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). These comprise the masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, and **lateral pterygoid**. Together, they execute elevation, depression, protrusion, retraction, and side-to-side grinding movements of the mandible.
steps.say: Four muscles of mastication derive from the first pharyngeal arch, innervated by mandibular nerve V3: masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, and lateral pterygoid.

steps.tx: The lateral pterygoid is the only muscle of mastication that opens the mouth. Arising by two heads from the greater wing of the sphenoid and lateral pterygoid plate, the **lateral pterygoid** inserts into the pterygoid fovea on the anterior neck of the mandible and the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint. Bilateral contraction pulls the condyles forward, depressing and protruding the chin.
steps.say: The lateral pterygoid is the only masticatory muscle that opens the mouth. Contracting bilaterally, it pulls the mandibular condyles and articular discs forward to open the jaw.

steps.tx: Unilateral contraction of the lateral pterygoid pulls the ipsilateral mandibular condyle forward and medially while the contralateral condyle rotates in place. This alternating action moves the chin to the opposite side, producing the essential grinding excursion of **mastication**. In unilateral trigeminal motor paralysis, pterygoid weakness causes the jaw to deviate towards the paralysed side on opening.
steps.say: Unilateral lateral pterygoid action pushes the chin to the opposite side during chewing. In trigeminal motor palsy, the jaw deviates toward the paralyzed side on opening.

steps.tx: During forceful local dental anaesthesia, an inferior alveolar nerve block targets the nerve as it enters the mandibular foramen. The needle traverses the pterygomandibular space between the ramus of the mandible and the **medial pterygoid** muscle. Inadvertent posterior penetration into the parotid gland can anesthetise the facial nerve, causing transient ipsilateral facial paralysis.
steps.say: Inferior alveolar nerve block infiltrates the pterygomandibular space. Inadvertent deep posterior injection into the parotid gland causes temporary facial nerve paralysis.
